zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical reference: the supplied NINJAL Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510, developed by Hideyuki Ohshima with assistance from Taichi Aida (CC BY 4.0; https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html). It was consulted after independent scan reading. The scan governs spelling, allographs, typography and lineation; the revised transcription and English notes are this review's own. Scan source: BnF Gallica / Bibliothèque nationale de France.

lines.note: Gijin denotes deities of the earth or land. The surviving letters and the preceding page's catchword support Gijin, not the draft's Gin; the Portuguese is da terra, not da uera.

runs.text: Huns paos que atraueßão de columna

lines.note: Gijiqij denotes wooden members running between columns. The initial G is abraded but still partly visible; the architectural gloss and following regional synonym support the recovered headword. Enlargement shows the right-hand s component of the ß ligature in atraueßão, rather than a lone ſ.

runs.text: a columna nos Zaxiquis ao longo dos Tatamis.

lines.note: Completes the architectural description: from column to column in rooms, along the tatami mats. Zaxiquis and Tatamis are Japanese terms embedded in the Portuguese explanation, distinct from the following regional usage label.
X. marks western regional usage, while the upper-region equivalent is Yoxejiqij. Cami is the regional name inside the Portuguese sentence; Yoxejiqij is the cited alternative form.

runs.text: Curar algũa doença vſando de muitos

lines.note: Gijut concerns treating an illness by many methods. The checked final t is retained, and the Portuguese list of means continues below.
Completes the list of methods, techniques, or medicines. A new example starts with the same Gijut, whose object particle appears on the next physical row.

runs.text: Vſar de todos os meos, & re-

lines.note: Gijut uo tçucuſu means exhausting the available therapeutic means. The particle is uo, not the draft's uio, and re- begins remedios below.
Completes remedios and the aim of curing an illness. This line closes the therapeutic-method entry.
Gin is the aromatic wood called aguila in this gloss, as the following incense-burning example makes clear. Ginuo taqu begins burning it for fragrance; the example's initial is G rather than C.
Completes placing aguila on the fire for its scent. The second example begins Ginuo tomu-, continued by ru on the next row.

runs.text: Perfumarſe com aguila, ou os veſtidos.

lines.note: Completes tomuru and describes perfuming oneself or one's clothes with the aromatic wood. This confirms the fragrance sense of aguila in this entry.
This separate Gin is a military camp. The final n of the headword is worn but supported by the repeated Ginuo; the example describes breaking or destroying the camp.
Completes Romper and begins another example for strengthening the camp. Catô has a circumflex, and its entire spelling belongs to the roman Japanese text, not partly to italic Portuguese.
Completes catô suru and gives catamuru as an alternative. The Portuguese explains fortifying or provisioning the camp.
Completes the camp object and starts expressions for taking up a camp position. Ginuo replaces the draft's garbled Cmnuo; the alternative gindoriuo continues below.
Completes gindoriuo suru, establishing a camp. Ginuo fiqu then introduces lifting or withdrawing the camp; Ale- begins its Portuguese translation.

runs.text: uantar o arrayal, ou ceßar a guerra.

lines.note: Completes Aleuantar and adds ceasing the war. The entry therefore distinguishes breaking a camp, fortifying it, establishing it, and withdrawing it.
Gin-ai denotes dust or small refuse, paraphrased by Chirichiri. The final Japanese syllable is ri, not the draft's ni; a further figurative sense begins with Im, without a secure line-end hyphen.
Completes Immunditia interior, inward impurity. The line provides the extended sense of Gin-ai rather than another physical kind of dust.

runs.text: O queimar o lugar, ou campo onde

lines.note: Ginbarai is defined here as burning the place or field occupied by an army. Queimar is the visible Portuguese verb; the definition is not replaced by a more familiar modern sense of the Japanese compound.
Completes the former army-camp location and gives Ginbaraiuo suru as the example. The spelling eſteue is retained as historical Portuguese.
Ginbu denotes labourers accompanying the army. The Portuguese begins a word divided a/carretão across the physical rows, without a secure hyphen.

runs.text: carretão no exercito, ou leuão fato.

lines.note: Completes acarretão: people who transport things in the army or carry baggage. Fato here belongs to the load-carrying description, not the modern English sense of 'fact'.
Ginbure is a proclamation for war. Ginbu- begins the example Ginbureuo suru, and the printed aguerra spacing is retained.

runs.text: Lançar pregão pera que ſe par-

lines.note: Completes the Japanese example and explains issuing a proclamation that people should depart. The Portuguese verb partão is divided after par-.
Completes the call to depart for war. This is the end of the proclamation entry.
Ginchǒqe is identified only as the name of a flower. The caron and hũa are supported by the scan; no botanical species is supplied from outside the entry.
Ginchǔ means within the army or camp. The damaged final vowel carries a caron over u, not the draft's unmarked a, and Ginno vchi confirms the interior-location sense.
Adds 'or camp' to the location definition. The short row completes Ginchǔ, not the next aromatic-wood entry.
Gincǒ is another name for the aromatic wood glossed aguila earlier in the column. The final caron is retained.
Gindachi is going or setting out for war. The beginning of the gloss is Oir, an O followed by the infinitive ir with close printed spacing, not the draft's Dir.
Gindoriuo suru means establishing a camp. The headword Gindori is supported by the surviving strokes and its clear repetition in the example, correcting Ciuidori.

runs.text: o arrayal, ou alojar o exercito.

lines.note: Completes establishing the camp or lodging the army. This is the full military-camping definition.
Gingai is dust and refuse, paraphrased by Chiri and acuta. The Portuguese adds straw and similar small litter.

The main text gives the figurative sense 'impurity'. At the far right, the parenthesis and exercito. are physically displaced completion material for Gingaye on the following row; they remain here in named far-right segments rather than being mistaken for part of the impurity gloss.

runs.text: O mudar o arrayal, ou poſto do

lines.note: Gingaye means changing the camp or army position. Its grammatical completion exercito. is printed at the far right of the preceding row and is preserved there, not silently moved into this line.
Ginja combines the aromatic wood and musk. The final vowel of almiſcre is e in the scan, correcting the draft's almiſcro while retaining the historical word.
Ginſui is scented water. The headword contains n followed by long s, not the draft's u, and the Portuguese confirms the fragrance-related grouping.
Gintǒ, explained by Coguchi, concerns the opening or front of battle. The Portuguese begins with conflict or the beginning of the battle and continues below.

runs.text: batalha. ¶ Item, Principio de hũ eſquadrão,

lines.note: Completes batalha and adds the front or beginning of a squadron. The abbreviated hũ remains unexpanded.

runs.text: ou manga de gente. ¶ Itẽ, Principo de hũa

lines.note: Adds a body of troops and then begins another sense, the head of an ordered group. The printed Principo is retained without supplying an expected extra i; hũa is damaged but compatible with the surviving marks and the following feminine ordem.

runs.text: ordem de gente como Cũgues que a companhão

lines.note: The example is an ordered procession of court nobles accompanying the ruler. Cũgues is the embedded Japanese designation; the visible a companhão spacing is preserved.
Completes the procession example: accompanying the Dairi when he goes out. The faint i in Dairi is retained from the surviving sequence; quando and fora correct the draft's false spacing and vowel.
Ginxo is the place where a camp has been established. The Japanese paraphrase begins Ginuo, not Ganuo; the Portuguese location description continues below.
Completes the place where the army is lodged. The damaged Portuguese reads alojado and exercito; Ginxouo ca- begins an example about enclosing or fortifying the camp.

runs.text: Cercar, ou fortalecer o lugar do

lines.note: Completes camayuru and explains surrounding or strengthening the camp site. The Portuguese verb is Cercar, not the draft's Cercur.
Completes the camp-site definition. The local arreyal vowel spelling is retained rather than harmonized with arrayal earlier in the column.

runs.text: Soldadeſca, ou os que eſtão no arrayal.

lines.note: Ginxu denotes the soldiery or people in the camp. The Portuguese explanation is complete on this row.

runs.text: Bonzos que vão com algum recado ao

lines.note: Ginzô denotes monks who carry a message to the army. The circumflex is retained, and the destination continues below.
Completes the destination of the monks' message. This short continuation belongs to Ginzô.
Giqen is land measurement or survey, paraphrased by Giuo xiruſu. The Portuguese object list continues with fields on the next row.
Adds fields to the survey definition. The line closes Giqen rather than beginning a new entry.
Giqidan means speaking directly or in person. The paraphrase begins Giqini with G, correcting the draft's C, and the Portuguese adverb continues below.

Completes presencialmente and gives a future statement about speaking in person. The tilde over a is discernible in Giqidãni, representing the nasal sequence before ni. The vowel after long s in mǒſozuru is abraded; the unmarked form is retained provisionally rather than supplying an expected long-vowel mark.
Completes the example's translation: 'I shall speak in person'. Em- on the preceding row and preſença here remain physically separate.

runs.text: Giqiden. Giqini tçutayuru, l, giqino ſo-

lines.note: Giqiden concerns direct transmission, explained by transmitting in person or direct consultation. The first Giqini has G, not the draft's C; the alternative ſo- continues below.
Dan completes sodan. The Portuguese explains saying or teaching in person; enſinar includes the i lost in the draft, and the abbreviated final adverb continues below.
Completes presencialmente and begins a Japanese example calling this the Apostles' directly transmitted teaching. Apoſtolono corrects the draft's Abostolono; giqidẽ retains its abbreviation tilde.

runs.text: Iſto he doctrina, ou tradição que os

lines.note: Completes gozaru and starts the Portuguese rendering as doctrine or tradition. The people who taught it and the manner of teaching follow below.
Completes the teaching passed on by the Apostles in person. The printed past-tense enſinarão is preserved rather than modernized.
Giqidǒ is a straight or right way, also understood as sound teaching. The Japanese word is michi, not the draft's nichi; doc- begins doctrina below.
Completes doctrina and qualifies it as good and upright. This supplies the ethical or doctrinal extension of the straight-way image.
Giqiguen denotes words spoken or heard in someone's presence. The locative expression is divided across the physical rows.
Completes em-preſença from the previous row. The short continuation closes the direct-hearing or direct-speaking definition.
Giqimu concerns personally administering one's landed holdings. The initial is G, not B; the Japanese paraphrase explicitly includes giqini, directly or in person.

runs.text: Gouernar, & adminiſtrar em peſſoa as pro-

lines.note: The Portuguese begins governing and administering one's own lands personally. Pro- continues as proprias on the next row.

runs.text: prias terras. i, Arrecadarem os Tonos dos

lines.note: Completes proprias terras and starts a more precise explanation: the lords themselves collect revenue from cultivators. Tonos is the Japanese lord-designation embedded in the Portuguese sentence.
Continues direct collection of the lands' income from the farmers. Immediatamente expresses the lack of an intermediary, as the next row makes explicit.

runs.text: ſuas terras ſem interuirem outros feitores, &c.

lines.note: Completes the explanation: no other stewards intervene. The printed interuirem spelling is retained, not repaired to a modern form.
Giqimuni suru gives the verbal expression for managing the holdings oneself. The Portuguese porſi is retained with its printed close spacing.
Completes the personal administration of one's revenues. This closes the detailed Giqimu entry.
Giqini is explicitly marked as an adverb meaning in person. The divided Gi- begins the example's repetition of the adverb.
Completes Giqini tatacǒ, fighting in person. The caron on the verb's final vowel is retained.
Giqinǒ and giqimu again concern direct administration, paraphrased by Suguni voſamuru. The scan restores the missing S in Suguni and long s in voſamuru; Gouer- continues below.

runs.text: narem peſſoa, ou adminiſtrar porſi ſuas terras.

lines.note: Completes governing in person or administering one's own lands. The close printed narem and porſi are retained rather than respaced from modern grammar alone.

runs.text: O ler cada dia oliuro de Xaca chuma-

lines.note: Giqiǒ denotes reading the named Buddhist scripture every day. Xaca is an embedded Japanese religious name. The scan prints chuma-, continuing as chuma-do below; its u is retained even though the naming construction would normally suggest chamado.

runs.text: do Foqeqiǒ como fazem os Bonzos.

lines.note: Completes the naming of Foqeqiǒ and says that monks perform this reading. The title's q letters and caron are visible; the draft's Fogeaiõ was not a separate book title.
Giqiǒja and giqiǒxa designate the monk responsible for that reading. The Japanese agent forms and their long-vowel marks are retained.

runs.text: officio deler cada dia o Foqeqiǒ.

lines.note: Completes the duty of reading Foqeqiǒ every day. The same title and caron recur, while the printed deler spacing remains unchanged.
Giqiſat is a letter sent directly, paraphrased by Giqino fuda. The recipients are specified on the next row.
The letter is addressed directly to a lord, teacher, or similar superior. Vt introduces the following example about the etiquette of such direct writing.
The Japanese example calls direct writing to a noble person discourteous. Giqiſatua includes the topic particle, and birǒ carries a caron.

runs.text: direitamente a homem nobre he deſcorteſia.

lines.note: Completes the etiquette statement: writing directly to a nobleman is discourtesy. This is the dictionary's stated convention, not a modern recommendation.
Atejǒ and tçuqejǒ introduce the contrasting indirect type of letter. The addressee arrangement is explained in the following rows.

runs.text: manda não immediatamente ao ſenhor, mas

lines.note: The letter is not sent straight to the lord. Mas introduces the intermediary who receives it instead.

runs.text: a algum que eſta junto delle pera que lha apre-

lines.note: It goes to someone near the lord so that this person may present it. The verb apreſente is divided after apre-.

runs.text: ſente, ou de parte dalgum negocio.

lines.note: Completes apreſente and adds reporting or conveying information about some business. The indirect-delivery explanation ends here.

runs.text: Nouas certas de couſas que hum vio,

lines.note: Giqiſǒ denotes reliable news of things personally witnessed. The initial G corrects the draft's C; a second evidential basis follows below.

runs.text: ou de que lhe veo carta, &c. No Cami ſe

lines.note: The reliable news may also come through a received letter. The sentence then introduces the term used in Cami, the upper-region label embedded in Portuguese.

Completes the regional comparison: in Cami the term is tißǒ. Its continuous italic appearance is retained across the whole word instead of isolating only the accented final vowel as Roman; the Japanese expression remains separately flagged for whole-word typeface review.

This separate Giqiſô means speaking or presenting a report in person. Enlargement distinguishes its circumflex from the caron on the preceding news entry Giqiſǒ, a distinction also present in the supplied lexical index. Giqini mǒſu agrees with the Portuguese, whose audience is specified below.

runs.text: preſencialmente ao Rey, ou a algum ſenhor

lines.note: The audience is a king or another great lord. The adjective qualifying the latter is on the following physical row.
Completes ſenhor grande, a great lord. This is a genuine short continuation, not bottom furniture.

Giqiſo is first given the same meaning and then an additional accusation sense. The scan has qi, not the draft's ji, and leaves the final o unmarked; the accusation definition continues at the opening of f254.

The separate catchword appears to print daa, with two a forms after d, although the continued body text on f254 reads dà. The literal doubled vowel is retained rather than silently harmonized; the worn final forms remain a nonblocking uncertainty.
